title: Conceptual Design of a Breakwater-Protected Offshore Floating Photovoltaic System: Layout Selection, Mooring and Anchoring Across Three European Sea Basins
content: Offshore floating photovoltaic (FPV) arrays can be sheltered by a surrounding floating breakwater, whose layout, anchoring and connection to the PV array then govern the design. This conceptual design study considers a 10 MWp FPV plant enclosed by modular concrete breakwater pontoons at three sites with mild (Baltic Sea, 16 m water depth), moderate (Mediterranean Sea, 38 m) and harsh (North Sea, 49 m) conditions. Initial mooring dimensions were derived from single-pontoon CFD results. Subsequent time-domain simulations of the complete moored breakwater ring provided mooring-line loads that informed a revision of the chain diameters, lengths and anchor positions.  Five layouts of equivalent PV area (circular, octagonal, triangular, elliptical and square) are rated against eight technical and economic criteria. The circular layout (diameter 346 m, 56 breakwater pontoons) ranks first, with the best rating in six of the eight criteria. For this layout, a multi-point catenary mooring with grade R4 stud link chains and driven steel piles is sized per site, including corrosion (40-year life) and marine growth allowances. The revised configurations use chain diameters of 107 mm for the Baltic Sea site and 87 mm for both the Mediterranean Sea and North Sea sites, with total chain lengths of 132.80 m, 192.60 m and 198.70 m, respectively.  A floating tubular transition element connected by pre-tensioned polypropylene ropes is proposed between breakwater and PV array. A structural model of a 20 × 14 module array gives rope safety factors of 3.2 and 4.4 against the supplier breaking loads. The revised anchoring configurations incorporate the findings of the system-level simulations, while detailed mooring-line dynamics, applicable limit-state checks and site-specific foundation design remain necessary.
